extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 7. The single most useful paragraph in the run is here: the Chicago Reading Room's directors resolve to put a building ON THE PUBLIC SQUARE, on a rent-free lease, for a reading room 'and for other public purposes' — a proposal, three weeks after the scene date, which is a negative claim about the square as it stood on 1835-07-01. The Marine Journal for July 7-16 is the run's fullest, twelve arrivals in ten days including a brig named John Kinzie.

claims.notes: THE PUBLIC SQUARE, WITH A BUILDING PROPOSED ON IT AND NOTHING ON IT YET — which is why this is the run's most valuable paragraph for a reconstruction dated 1835-07-01. The directors resolve that a joint-stock company should put up a building on the square under a RENT-FREE LEASE, for a reading room 'and for other public purposes', paying its investors back out of the rents. Three things follow. On the scene date the square carries no reading room and no such building; the square is understood to be leasable ground a private company could build on; and a committee is named to pursue it. WHERE THE SQUARE'S NAME IS CUT: the transcription reads 'on th iyware free of rent' — 'th[e … Sq]uare', with the qualifier destroyed. It is read as the Public Square because this is a public-purposes building on rent-free public ground in a town with one such square, and because the same run separately places a dwelling against 'the Public Square' (1835-07-04). The reading is stated here rather than left to look certain. 'Lieut. J. Al[len]' is completed and bracketed; a serving lieutenant on a civic committee is itself worth noting in a garrison town.

claims.notes: THE FULLEST PORT COLUMN OF THE RUN: twelve arrivals and eight clearances between July 7 and July 16 — roughly a vessel a day working the river mouth three weeks after the scene date. FIVE CARGOES OF LUMBER OR FLOUR, and the trade pattern is now unmistakable: St. Joseph, Root River, Michigan City, Milwaukee and Detroit on the short runs, Buffalo on the long one. A BRIG NAMED JOHN KINZIE clears for Buffalo on the 10th, which is worth a line of its own: the man this run documents four times as a merchant, steamboat agent and landlord also has a lake brig carrying his name. The names of masters ('Gauchnois', 'Wagstaff', 'Barker') are single-pass OCR of a list set in small type and are bracketed where completed.

claims.notes: THE AUCTION ROOM'S PLACEMENT SET CLEAN AT LAST — 'David Carver's old stand, South Water street' in one unbroken phrase, where the three earlier printings each lost part of it. It also shows what the room was FOR three weeks after opening: a second notice in the same column offers to dispose of TOWN LOTS by public or private sale, so the auctioneer is trading in real estate as well as goods in the summer of the land boom. The 'doors west of J. Wright's' half of the address is absent from this printing and is carried by 1835-07-04's.

claims.notes: THE HARDWARE AND FARM-IMPLEMENT SHELF OF A CHICAGO STORE IN JULY 1835, listed by the piece: cut nails and spikes, iron, cast and German steel, patent horse shoes, mill irons, cross-cut saws, anvils, vices, crowbars, rakes, scythe snaths, riveted forks, shovels, spades, hoes, grass scythes, hay and manure forks, scythe stones and rifles. That is a directly usable inventory for a reconstruction that dresses yards, sheds and shopfronts. ATTRIBUTION IS PARTIAL AND IS SAID SO: only the last group carries a signature (Philo Carpenter) and only the wines carry Hubbard & Co.'s; the nails and the implements sit in spans the segmenter has cut away from whatever signed them, and they are recorded on Carpenter's business as the nearest signature in the same column. The IRON AND NAILS line dated June 13 matches the unsigned hardware card 1835-06-13 could not attribute either — the same stock, still unclaimed after five weeks.

claims.notes: FOUR THOUSAND LIGHTS OF WINDOW GLASS AND SASH MADE BY HAND, on consignment in one Chicago store — and in the same column, Saranac window glass and TWO named crown glasses, New York and Brooklyn, sold at the company's prices plus freight. This is the best glazing evidence in the corpus and it bears directly on how this project treats windows: hand-made sash, glass shipped in by named works, and a quantity (4,000 lights) that says how much building was going on. Three consignments are quoted together because they run together in the column; only the first carries a signature, Jno. Wilson & Co., and only its goods are attributed.

claims.notes: THE ESTRAY OF 1835-07-11, REPRINTED WITH THE DESCRIPTION LEGIBLE: a dark chestnut horse of about SIXTEEN HANDS, unmarked and unbranded. The earlier printing carried the finder's address — John K. Clark, eight miles up the North Branch — and lost the animal; this one carries the animal and loses him. Sixteen hands is a large horse for the frontier and is the only documented measurement of a live animal in this corpus, which matters to a project that puts horses and waggons in its streets at a stated scale.
